## Interaction of the Canada Labour Code with Other Laws and Regulations

### Federal Labour Standards and Provincial Laws

The Canada Labour Code establishes federal labour standards that apply to employees working in federally regulated businesses. However, it does not supersede provincial labour laws. Instead, the Code and provincial laws operate in parallel, creating a layered system of labour protections.
"Part III of the Canada  Labour Code talks about federal labour standards. These set out the  employment conditions for hours of work, payment of wages, leaves, vacation,  holidays, and more. These standards apply to employees working in federally  regulated businesses." This passage highlights the scope of the federal labour standards outlined in the Code. It clarifies that these standards are specifically for employees in federally regulated sectors, leaving provincial laws to govern employees in provincially regulated businesses.

This interaction has implications for individuals and organizations. Employees working in federally regulated businesses are entitled to the federal labour standards, while those in provincially regulated businesses are subject to the provincial standards. Employers operating in both federally and provincially regulated sectors must comply with both sets of labour laws.

### Regulations Made Under the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code empowers the Governor in Council to make regulations for carrying out the purposes of the Part. These regulations can address a wide range of labour standards issues, including record-keeping requirements, the designation of industrial establishments, the calculation of wages, and the establishment of consultative committees.
"Section 264 (1) The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Part and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations (a) requiring employers to keep records of wages, vacations, holidays and overtime of employees and of other particulars relevant to the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof..." This section explicitly states the regulatory authority granted by the Code. It outlines the broad scope of regulations that can be made, including requirements for employers to maintain detailed records of employee compensation and benefits.

These regulations have significant implications for organizations. Employers are legally obligated to comply with the regulations made under the Code, which can impose substantial administrative burdens. Conversely, regulations can also provide clarity and guidance on the application of the Code's provisions.

### Other Laws and Regulations

The Canada Labour Code also interacts with other federal and provincial laws and regulations. For example, it is subject to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantees certain fundamental rights to employees. It also interacts with other laws related to health and safety, workplace harassment, and human rights.
"Section 166 In this Part, collective agreement means an agreement in writing containing terms or conditions of employment of employees, including provisions with reference to rates of pay, hours of work and settlement by a third party of disagreements arising in the application of the agreement, between (a) an employer or an employers’ organization acting on behalf of an employer, and (b) a trade union acting on behalf of the employees in collective bargaining or as a party to an agreement with the employer or employers’ organization..." This passage illustrates the Code's relationship with collective agreements, which are governed by separate legislation but are nonetheless subject to the overarching principles of the Labour Code.

This interaction with other laws and regulations has implications for both individuals and organizations. Employees can rely on the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to challenge unfair labour practices. Employers must comply with all applicable laws and regulations, including those related to health and safety and workplace harassment.

### Implications for Certain Individuals and Organizations

**Vulnerable Workers:
"Employees face a range of barriers to enforcing their rights  through individual complaints. For example, employees who file complaints must  provide their name, which is shared with their employer during the complaints  process. Studies demonstrate that, in most cases, complaints are filed by  employees who no longer work for the employer targeted by the complaints because of fear of reprisals..." This passage highlights the challenges faced by vulnerable workers, such as temporary foreign workers and temporary workers, in enforcing their rights through individual complaints. The fear of reprisal often prevents them from coming forward with concerns.

"Employers and employer organizations told  us that non-compliance is often due to a lack of awareness. In particular, they  said that while the majority of large employers understand their obligations,  smaller employers may not." This indicates that small employers may face particular challenges in complying with the Code's provisions due to a lack of awareness of their obligations.

**Federally Regulated Businesses:
"These standards apply to employees working in federally  regulated businesses." This clarifies that the federal labour standards apply specifically to employees in federally regulated sectors, which have a different regulatory framework than provincially regulated businesses.

In conclusion, the Canada Labour Code operates within a complex legal framework that includes provincial laws, regulations made under the Code, and other federal and provincial laws. This interaction has significant implications for individuals and organizations, particularly vulnerable workers, small employers, and those operating in federally regulated businesses. Ensuring compliance with all applicable labour laws and regulations is crucial for protecting the rights of workers and promoting a fair and equitable labour market.

## Employer Responsibilities for Hazardous Substances in Non-Controlled Workplaces

### Balancing Control and Employee Protection

The Canada Labour Code places significant responsibility on employers to protect employees from hazardous substances, even when the workplace or activity is not directly controlled by the employer. This requires a delicate balance between maintaining control over work activities and fulfilling the duty to ensure employee safety.

#### Employer Obligations Regarding Hazardous Substances

Section 125(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines specific duties employers have regarding hazardous substances, extending to activities not directly controlled by them,
"...to the extent that the employer controls the activity..." This means that even when an employer doesn't have direct control, they are still obligated to take steps to protect their employees from hazards they influence.
"...ensure that concentrations of hazardous substances in the work place are controlled in accordance with prescribed standards..."

This indicates that employers must actively manage hazardous substances within their sphere of influence. This includes controlling concentrations, storing and handling substances properly, and identifying hazardous products.

Furthermore, employers are required to provide employees with safety data sheets (SDS) for hazardous products they may be exposed to. This ensures that employees have access to crucial information about the risks associated with these substances and how to protect themselves.
"...make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act..."

This provision highlights the employer's responsibility to inform employees about the hazards they face.

#### Employer Responsibilities for Non-Controlled Workplaces

The Code extends these responsibilities to workplaces not directly controlled by the employer,
"...to the extent that the employer controls the activity..." This is crucial for situations where an employer influences work activities but doesn't have direct operational control.

Employers must investigate and assess employee exposure to hazardous substances, often with the assistance of the workplace committee or health and safety representative. This proactive approach allows employers to identify and address potential risks.
"...where employees may be exposed to hazardous substances, investigate and assess the exposure in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the work place committee or the health and safety representative..."

This demonstrates the employer's obligation to actively monitor and manage hazards even in non-controlled environments.

#### Employer Cooperation and Consultation

The Code also emphasizes the importance of employer cooperation and consultation with health and safety committees and representatives. This collaborative approach ensures that employee concerns are addressed and that safety measures are effective.

Employers are required to consult with these committees on the implementation and monitoring of hazard prevention programs. This ensures that safety measures are tailored to the specific hazards present in the workplace.
"...consult with the work place committee or the health and safety representative on the implementation and monitoring of programs developed in consultation with the policy committee."

This highlights the employer's responsibility to engage with employees in developing and implementing safety measures.

### Conclusion

Employers must strike a balance between maintaining control over work activities and fulfilling their responsibility to protect employees from hazardous substances, even in non-controlled workplaces. This requires a proactive approach to managing hazards, providing employees with information, and collaborating with health and safety committees and representatives. The Canada Labour Code clearly outlines these obligations, emphasizing the employer's paramount duty to ensure employee safety.

### Primary Purpose

The primary purpose of requiring employers to provide safety data sheet (SDS) information to medical professionals in emergency situations is to facilitate accurate and timely medical diagnosis and treatment of employees who have been exposed to hazardous products. This ensures that medical personnel have the necessary details about the substance involved to provide appropriate care.

### Legal Basis and Specific Requirements

Section 125.2(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines this employer duty:
"An employer shall, in respect of every work place controlled by the employer and, in respect of every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls that activity, provide, in respect of any hazardous product to which an employee may be exposed, as soon as is practicable in the circumstances, any information that is included in the safety data sheet that is in the employer’s possession for the hazardous product to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests that information for the purpose of making a medical diagnosis of, or rendering medical treatment to, an employee in an emergency."

This section mandates that employers must furnish SDS information to medical professionals promptly when an employee experiences an emergency related to hazardous product exposure. The provision for "as soon as is practicable in the circumstances" acknowledges that immediate access may not always be feasible but emphasizes the urgency of the provision.

### Confidentiality Considerations

While the employer is obligated to provide SDS information, Section 125.2(2) addresses confidentiality:
"Any physician or other prescribed medical professional to whom information is provided by an employer pursuant to subsection (1) shall keep confidential any information specified by the employer as being confidential, except for the purpose for which it is provided."

This provision ensures that while the SDS information is provided for emergency medical care, any information the employer designates as confidential will be treated accordingly, except for the immediate medical needs of the employee.

### Overall Goal

The overarching goal of this employer duty is to empower medical professionals with the critical information contained in SDSs to make informed medical decisions and provide effective treatment to employees who have been exposed to hazardous substances in an emergency. This directly supports the employer's broader responsibility to ensure the health and safety of their employees.

## Penalty System and Existing Enforcement Measures

### General Offence Penalties

Section 148 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the general offence penalties. It states,
"Subject to this section, every person who contravenes a provision of this Part is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $100,000." This penalty system directly relates to existing enforcement measures by providing a legal framework for responding to violations of the Labour Code.

The penalty structure differentiates between indictment and summary conviction, reflecting the severity of the offence. Indictment, typically for more serious offences, carries a higher potential fine and imprisonment. Summary conviction, for less serious offences, carries a lower fine. This tiered system allows for proportionate responses to different levels of Labour Code violations.

### Offences and Punishment: Procedure

Section 257 of the Canada Labour Code details the procedural aspects of offences and punishments. It mentions that
"Proceedings in respect of an offence under this Part may be instituted at any time within but not later than three years after the time when the subject-matter of the proceedings arose." This time limit is an existing enforcement measure that ensures timely action is taken against Labour Code violations.

Furthermore, Section 257(3) specifies that
"No proceeding against a director of a corporation in respect of an offence under this Part shall be instituted except with the consent of the Minister." This provision introduces a gatekeeping mechanism for prosecutions against corporate directors, indicating an existing enforcement process involving ministerial approval.

### Offences and Punishment: Offences and punishment

Section 256 of the Canada Labour Code elaborates on the offences and punishments. It states,
"Every person is guilty of an offence who (a) contravenes any provision of this Part or the regulations, other than a provision of Division IX, subsection 239.1(2), 239.2(1), 251.001(9) or 252(2) or any regulation made under section 227 or paragraph 264(1)(a) or (a.1); (b) contravenes any order made under this Part or the regulations; or (c) discharges, threatens to discharge or otherwise discriminates against a person because that person (i) has testified or is about to testify in any proceedings or inquiry taken or had under this Part, or (ii) has given any information to the Minister or the Head regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of an employee." This section provides a comprehensive list of offences under the Labour Code, which are the targets of existing enforcement measures.

The penalty system outlined in Section 256 further details the fines applicable to different levels of conviction. It states,
"Every person who is guilty of an offence under subsection (1) is liable on summary conviction (a) in the case of an employer that is a corporation, (i) for a first offence, to a fine of not more than $50,000, (ii) for a second offence, to a fine of not more than $100,000, and (iii) for each subsequent offence, to a fine of not more than $250,000; and (b) in all other cases, (i) for a first offence, to a fine of not more than $10,000, (ii) for a second offence, to a fine of not more than $20,000, and (iii) for each subsequent offence, to a fine of not more than $50,000." This tiered penalty system is directly linked to existing enforcement measures, providing a range of financial penalties for different levels of Labour Code violations.

### Regulations and Penalty Amounts

Section 270 of the Canada Labour Code discusses the power of the Governor in Council to make regulations. It states,
"The Governor in Council may make regulations (a) designating as a violation that may be proceeded with in accordance with this Part (i) the contravention of any specified provision of Part II or III or of any regulations made under those Parts, (ii) the contravention of any direction, or of any direction of any specified class of directions, issued under any provision of Part II or of any regulations made under that Part, (iii) the contravention of any order, or of any order of any specified class of orders, made or issued under any provision of Part II or III or of any regulations made under those Parts, or (iv) the failure to comply with any condition, or with any condition of any specified class of conditions, of a permit issued under section 176; (b) respecting the determination of, or the method of determining, the amount payable as the penalty for each violation, penalties which may be different for individuals and for other persons and departments; (c) respecting the circumstances under which, the criteria by which and the manner in which a penalty may be reduced; (d) respecting the determination of a lesser amount than the penalty imposed that may be paid in complete satisfaction of the penalty if paid within the time and manner prescribed by regulation; (e) respecting the service of documents required or authorized under this Part, including the manner and proof of service and the circumstances under which documents are deemed to be served; (f) prescribing the method of calculating and determining the regular rate of wages for the purpose of section 288; (g) prescribing anything that by this Part is to be prescribed; and (h) generally, for carrying out the purposes and provisions of this Part." This section highlights how regulations can further refine the penalty system by specifying penalty amounts for particular violations.

Section 270(2) further clarifies the upper limit on penalties, stating,
"The amount that may be determined under any regulations made under paragraph (1)(b) as the penalty for a violation may not exceed $250,000." This cap on penalties is an existing enforcement measure that provides a clear limit on the financial consequences of Labour Code violations.

### Offences — Employers

Section 256(2) specifically addresses offences committed by employers. It states,
"Every employer that contravenes any provision of Division IX, subsection 239.1(2) or 239.2(1) or any regulation made under section 227 is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction and liable to a fine of not more than $250,000." This provision directly relates to existing enforcement measures by establishing a penalty for employers who violate Labour Code provisions.

### Offences — Employers (Failure to Keep Records)

Section 256(3) provides another example of an offence committed by employers and its corresponding penalty. It states,
"Every employer who (a) fails to keep any record that, by subsection 252(2) or any regulation made under paragraph 264(1)(a) or (a.1), the employer is required to keep, or (b) refuses to make available for examination by the Head at any reasonable time any such record kept by the employer, is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine of not more than $1,000 for each day during which the refusal or failure continues." This provision introduces a penalty for employers who fail to maintain required records or refuse to make them available for inspection, representing an existing enforcement measure focused on record-keeping compliance.

In summary, the penalty system established under this Part of the Canada Labour Code is deeply intertwined with existing enforcement measures. It provides a legal framework for responding to Labour Code violations through tiered penalties based on the severity of the offence and the level of conviction. Existing enforcement measures, such as time limits for proceedings, ministerial consent for prosecutions against corporate directors, and the power to create regulations for specific penalty amounts, all work in conjunction with the penalty system to ensure compliance with the Labour Code.

## Exclusion of "No Representation" Option on Ballots

### Circumstances for Exclusion

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific situations where the Board can exclude the option for employees to indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union on the ballots during a representation vote. This exclusion occurs when the outcome of a previous representation vote does not yield majority support for a single trade union.

#### Scenario: No Majority Support for One Union

The Board can exclude the "no representation" option if
"...the employees in a unit have cast ballots in favour of all trade unions involved in a representation vote totalling more than fifty per cent of all the ballots cast but have not given majority support to one trade union in that vote and, as a result, a second or subsequent representation vote is required..."
"Notwithstanding subsection (2), where the employees in a unit have cast ballots in favour of all trade unions involved in a representation vote totalling more than fifty per cent of all the ballots cast but have not given majority support to one trade union in that vote and, as a result, a second or subsequent representation vote is required, the Board shall not be required to include the choice referred to in subsection (2) in the ballots for the second or subsequent vote."

This passage directly addresses the exclusion of the "no representation" option. It states that if a previous vote resulted in more than fifty percent of the ballots cast favoring all unions but no single union receiving a majority, then the Board is not required to include the "no representation" option on subsequent votes. This is because the outcome of the first vote did not clearly indicate a preference for any single union.

### Exception for Initial Certification Votes

There is an exception to this rule for the initial certification vote. When a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where no other trade union is currently the bargaining agent, the Board must include a "no representation" option on the ballots.
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken on an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, the Board shall include on the ballots a choice whereby an employee may indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots."

### Prosecutor's Recovery Options

According to Section 289 of the Canada Labour Code, if a person or a department pays the penalty set out in a notice of violation, the person or the department is considered to have committed the violation and proceedings are ended. "Where a person is convicted of an offence under this Part and the fine that is imposed is not paid when required, the prosecutor may, by filing the conviction, enter as a judgment the amount of the fine and costs, if any, in a superior court of the province in which the trial was held, and the judgment is enforceable against the person in the same manner as if it were a judgment rendered against the person in that court in civil proceedings."

This passage explains that if the fine is not paid, the prosecutor can initiate legal proceedings to obtain a judgment for the unpaid fine. This is done by filing the conviction in a superior court. The judgment then becomes enforceable against the person who failed to pay, in the same way as a judgment rendered in civil proceedings. This provides the prosecutor with a robust method for recovering unpaid fines.

Furthermore, Section 291 clarifies the nature of a penalty:
"A penalty constitutes a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and is recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction."

This statement establishes that a penalty is essentially a debt owed to the Crown. Therefore, the prosecutor can pursue recovery of the unpaid fine through the Federal Court or any other court with jurisdiction over debts owed to Her Majesty.

### Certificate of Unpaid Debt

Section 292 also mentions the Head's ability to issue a certificate:
"The Head may issue a certificate certifying the unpaid amount of any debt referred to in subsection 291(1)."

This certificate serves as a formal confirmation of the unpaid debt and can be used in court proceedings to obtain a judgment.

### Registration of the Certificate

Section 292 further elaborates on the enforceability of the certificate:
"Registration in the Federal Court or in any other court of competent jurisdiction of a certificate issued under subsection (1) has the same force and effect as a judgment of that court for a debt of the amount specified in the certificate and all related registration costs."

This indicates that if the certificate is registered in a court, it gains the same legal force as a judgment, allowing the prosecutor to enforce the debt against the person who failed to pay the fine.

### Entitlement to Leave for Reserve Force Members

The primary purpose of the provisions related to leaves of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code is to grant certain employees who are members of the reserve force the right to take leaves of absence for specific military operations, activities, and training. This ensures that reserve force members can fulfill their duties while still maintaining their employment.
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence..."

This section clearly establishes the entitlement to leave for reserve force members, outlining the minimum continuous employment requirement and the types of operations and activities for which leave can be granted.

### Entitlement to Leave for Other Military and Civil Duties

Beyond reserve force operations, the provisions also extend leave entitlements to employees called out on service for various military and civil duties.
"(d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection."

This passage details the various military and civil duties for which leave can be granted, including training, duties performed on active service, service in aid of civil power, and treatment for health problems resulting from service.

### Maximum Duration of Leave

While the provisions grant leave entitlements, they also include a maximum duration to prevent excessive disruptions to employment.
"Leaves taken by an employee under paragraphs (1)(a) to (d) can total no more than an aggregate of 24 months in any 60-month period."

This limitation ensures that reserve force members and employees called out on service do not take leaves that are unduly long and cause significant hardship to their employers.

### Exceptions to Leave Entitlement

The provisions also specify certain exceptions to the leave entitlement.
"Despite subsection (1), an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if, in the opinion of the Head, it would adversely affect public health or safety or would cause undue hardship to the employer if the employee, as an individual or as a member of a class of employees, were to take leave."

This section grants broad authority to the Governor in Council to create detailed rules and procedures for implementing the leave entitlements, addressing various aspects such as defining operations, specifying activities, and outlining exceptions.

In summary, the general purpose of the provisions related to leaves of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code is to provide a framework for granting employees who are members of the reserve force and those called out on service the right to take leaves for specific military and civil duties, while also setting limits on the duration of such leaves and providing for certain exceptions. This passage highlights that employer actions, such as actively opposing union certification drives, can lead the Board to order a representation vote to gauge the employees' true preference. An employer must apply to the Head, who will then decide whether to grant the permit based on the specific circumstances of the workplace and the well-being of the employees. The permit specifies the number of additional hours employees may work.

### Justification and Notice Requirements
"No permit may be issued under subsection (1) unless the applicant has satisfied the Head (a) that exceptional circumstances exist that justify the working of additional hours; (b) that the employer had posted a notice of the application for the permit, for at least 30 days before its proposed effective date, in places readily accessible to the affected class of employees where they were likely to see it; and (c) that the employer had informed the trade union in writing of the application for the permit, if those employees are represented by a trade union." ### Duration and Additional Hour Specification

"A permit under subsection (1) may specify either (a) the total of the number of additional hours in excess of the maximum hours specified in or prescribed under section 171 or by regulations made under section 175, or (b) the additional hours that may be worked in any day and in any week during the period of the permit." This indicates that the permit can either specify the total number of extra hours allowed or the maximum number of extra hours that can be worked per day or week during the permit's validity.

### Reporting Requirements
"If a permit has been issued under this section, the employer for whom or on whose behalf the permit was issued shall report in writing to the Head, within 15 days after the expiration of the period specified in the permit or within such time as the Head may fix in the permit, stating the number of employees who worked in excess of the maximum hours specified in or prescribed under section 171 or by regulations made under section 175 and the number of additional hours each of them worked." This section outlines the mandatory reporting requirements for employers who receive an excess hours permit. The employer must submit a written report to the Head within 15 days after the permit expires, detailing the number of employees who worked beyond the maximum hours and the number of additional hours each of them worked.

## Additional Implications
"Obtaining a permit does not exempt the employer from the obligation to pay overtime. The employer must report in writing to the Head within 15 days after the permit expires or at another date specified in the permit. The report must show the number of:  employees who worked more than 48 hours in a week, and additional hours in a week each employee worked..." This further clarifies that while a permit allows for exceeding the maximum hours, employers are still obligated to pay overtime for hours worked beyond 48 in a week. ## Factors Considered by the Board When Deciding on Revocation or Declaration of Inability to Represent

### Application for Revocation of Certification

#### Majority of Employees No Longer Wishing Representation
"If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit."

This section explicitly states the primary factor the Board considers when deciding whether to revoke certification. It highlights the Board's need to be
"...satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them..." This determination is made after an inquiry, which can take the form of a representation vote or other methods deemed appropriate by the Board. If this majority is found, the Board issues an order revoking the certification or declaring the bargaining agent no longer entitled to represent the employees.

#### Failure to Make Reasonable Effort to Enter into a Collective Agreement
"If no collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force, an order shall not be made under paragraph (1)(a) in relation to the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit."

This subsection introduces an additional factor when no collective agreement is in force. It specifies that an order revoking certification cannot be made unless the Board is convinced that the bargaining agent has
"...failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit." This indicates that the Board assesses the bargaining agent's commitment to reaching a collective agreement as a crucial element in its decision-making process.

### Application for Declaration of Inability to Represent

#### Failure to Make Reasonable Effort to Enter into a Collective Agreement (When No Collective Agreement is in Force)
"If no collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force, an order shall not be made under paragraph (1)(a) in relation to the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit."

This subsection reiterates the importance of the bargaining agent's efforts to reach a collective agreement when no existing one is in force. It clarifies that an order declaring the bargaining agent not entitled to represent employees cannot be made unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has
"...failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit."

#### Failure to Make Reasonable Effort to Enter into a Collective Agreement (When a Collective Agreement is in Force)
"Where the Board is satisfied that a trade union has an established practice of admitting persons to membership without regard to the eligibility requirements of its charter, constitution or by-laws, the Board may disregard those requirements in determining whether a person is a member of a trade union."

While not directly addressing the revocation of certification or declaration of inability to represent, this section touches upon the Board's consideration of a union's membership practices. It states that the Board may disregard membership requirements if the union has a history of admitting members without regard to the charter's stipulations. This suggests that the Board assesses the legitimacy and adherence to union rules as a factor in determining whether a union can legitimately represent employees.

#### Failure to Make Reasonable Effort to Enter into a Collective Agreement (During a Strike or Lockout)
"An application under subsection (1) or (3) must not, except with the consent of the Board, be made in respect of the bargaining agent for employees in a bargaining unit during a strike or lockout of those employees that is not prohibited by this Part."

This subsection addresses the Board's consideration of the bargaining agent's efforts to reach a collective agreement during a strike or lockout. It states that an application for revocation of certification or declaration of inability to represent cannot be made during a strike or lockout unless the Board consents. This implies that the Board assesses whether the bargaining agent has made a reasonable effort to reach a collective agreement despite the industrial action.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Board decide not to file a copy of its order or decision in a court?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances Where the Board May Not File a Copy of its Order or Decision in Court

### Section 23(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose."

This section outlines the general obligation of the Board to file a copy of its order or decision in the Federal Court upon request. However, it provides two specific circumstances where the Board may decline to do so. 

The first circumstance is when the Board believes there is
"...no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision..." This suggests that if the Board has reason to believe that the employer will adhere to the order without further prompting, it may deem the filing in court unnecessary. 

The second circumstance is when the Board has
"...other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose." This is a broader exception, allowing the Board to forgo filing if it perceives no practical benefit to doing so. The Board's "good reason" could encompass various factors, such as the order being self-executing or the potential for the order to be readily enforced through other means.



### Section 23(2) of the Canada Labour Code
"Where the Board files a copy of any order or decision in the Federal Court pursuant to subsection (1), it shall specify in writing to the Court that the copy of the order or decision is filed pursuant to that subsection and, where the Board so specifies, the copy of the order or decision shall be accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding."

This section clarifies the procedure when the Board decides *not* to file in court. It states that the Board must inform the Court in writing that the filing is being made pursuant to subsection (1). This ensures transparency and allows the Court to understand the Board's rationale. However, it does not specify any other circumstances under which the Board may choose not to file in court.



### Section 22(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act."

This section emphasizes the finality of the Board's orders and decisions. It states that they are generally not subject to court review, except under very specific circumstances outlined in the Federal Courts Act. This suggests that the Board has considerable discretion in deciding whether or not to file an order in court, and it is not obligated to do so in most cases.



### Section 156(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This section reiterates the finality of the Board's orders and decisions, echoing the sentiment expressed in Section 22(1). It reinforces the Board's discretion in deciding whether or not to file an order in court, as it is not required to do so in most instances.



In summary, the Board can decide not to file a copy of its order or decision in court under two main circumstances: when it has no indication of failure or likelihood of compliance with the order, or when it has other good reason why the filing in court would serve no useful purpose. However, the Board is generally obligated to file in court upon request, unless it has a valid reason not to do so. The finality of the Board's orders and decisions also gives the Board considerable discretion in this matter.

### Section 36(1)(c): Substitution as a Party to Existing Collective Agreements

Section 36(1)(c) directly addresses the implications for a newly certified trade union when it assumes the bargaining agent role in an existing collective agreement. It states:
"...the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto..."

This passage is crucial because it clarifies the immediate effect of certification on existing collective agreements. When a new trade union is certified, it "is substituted" as a party to the existing agreement. This means that the previous bargaining agent is effectively removed from the agreement, and the newly certified union steps into their place.

### Section 36(2): Requirement to Commence Collective Bargaining

Section 36(2) outlines the trade union's right and obligation to initiate collective bargaining following certification, particularly when it becomes a party to an existing collective agreement. It specifies:
"Where, pursuant to paragraph (1)(c), a trade union is substituted as a party to a collective agreement, the trade union may, within three months after the date on which it is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit affected by the collective agreement, require the employer who is a party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This section is significant because it grants the newly certified union the power to demand that the employer begin collective bargaining. The timeframe for this demand is within three months of certification. The union can request either a renewal or revision of the existing collective agreement or the negotiation of a completely new one. This ensures that the newly certified union has the opportunity to address the needs and concerns of the bargaining unit's employees.

### Section 36(3): Limitation on Subsection (2)

Section 36(3) provides a limitation on the requirement to commence collective bargaining outlined in subsection (2). It states:
"Subsection (2) does not apply to a trade union certified as a result of an application made under section 24.1."

This passage is important because it excludes a specific type of certification from the three-month requirement to commence collective bargaining. A trade union certified as a result of an application made under section 24.1 is not subject to this requirement. ## The Minister's Role in Strike and Lockout Notice

### Section 87.2: Notice to Employer and Trade Union

The Minister plays a crucial role in the process of a trade union or employer giving notice of a potential strike or lockout. Section 87.2 outlines the specific requirements for such notices and the Minister's involvement.
"...not prohibited by this Part has occurred, a trade union must give notice to the employer, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a strike will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."

This quote directly states that the Minister is required to receive a copy of a trade union's notice of a potential strike. This ensures that the Minister is informed of the impending action and can potentially intervene or facilitate resolution.
"Unless a strike not prohibited by this Part has occurred, an employer must give notice to the trade union, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a lockout will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."

Similarly, this quote indicates that the Minister is also required to receive a copy of an employer's notice of a potential lockout. This further emphasizes the Minister's role in being kept informed of potential disruptions to operations.

### Section 87.3: New Notice

Section 87.3 addresses the scenario where a strike or lockout does not occur on the date indicated in a notice. It outlines the requirement for a new notice to be given.
"Unless the parties agree otherwise in writing, where no strike or lockout occurs on the date indicated in a notice given pursuant to subsection (1) or (2), a new notice of at least seventy-two hours must be given by the trade union or the employer if they wish to initiate a strike or lockout."

This quote highlights the Minister's role in receiving a copy of any new notice given after a previously announced strike or lockout has been averted. This ensures that the Minister remains aware of any changes in the potential for industrial action.

### Section 87.4: Maintenance of Activities

Section 87.4 details the obligations of employers, trade unions, and employees during a strike or lockout. It also outlines the process for entering into an agreement regarding compliance with these obligations and the Minister's involvement.
"(2) An employer and a trade union must, no later than 15 days after the day on which notice to bargain collectively has been given, enter into an agreement with respect to compliance with subsection (1) that sets out (a) the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods that they consider necessary to continue in the event of a strike or a lockout; and (b) the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production, including the approximate number of those employees that, in the opinion of the employer and the trade union, would be required for that purpose."

This quote states that an employer and trade union must enter into an agreement regarding compliance with the maintenance of activities obligations within 15 days of giving notice to bargain collectively. The Minister is required to receive a copy of this agreement.
"Immediately after entering into the agreement, the employer and the trade union must file a copy of it with the Minister and the Board."

This quote explicitly states that the employer and trade union must file a copy of the agreement with both the Minister and the Board. This ensures that the Minister is officially informed of the agreement and can potentially intervene or facilitate resolution.

### Section 87.5: Referral to the Board

Section 87.5 outlines the Minister's authority to refer any question with respect to the application of subsection (1) to the Board.
"The Minister may refer to the Board any question with respect to whether an agreement entered into by the employer and the trade union is sufficient to ensure that subsection (1) is complied with."

This quote directly states that the Minister has the power to refer any question regarding the sufficiency of an agreement to the Board. This allows the Board to make a determination on whether the agreement is adequate to prevent an immediate and serious danger to public safety or health.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can an employee's complaint under the Canada Labour Code be suspended or not permitted?
individual_results.answer:
## Suspension of Complaint

### Circumstances Leading to Suspension by the Board

Section 241.1 outlines the Board's power to suspend consideration of a complaint. It states:
"If the Board is satisfied that the complainant must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint referred to it under subsection 241(3), it may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part."

This indicates that the Board can suspend a complaint if it deems necessary for the complainant to take specific actions before the Board can proceed. These measures are detailed in section 241.1(2):
"If the Board suspends consideration of a complaint, the Board shall notify the complainant in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the complainant must take; and (b) the period within which they must take those measures."

The suspension concludes when the Board is satisfied that the specified measures have been taken, as per section 241.1(3):
"The suspension ends when, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken."

Similarly, Section 246.2 mirrors this power of suspension, stating:
"If the Board is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint made under subsection 246.1(1), it may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part."

### Circumstances Leading to Rejection of Complaint

Section 241.2 details the circumstances under which the Board may reject a complaint. It lists several reasons, including:
"(a) if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, (ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the complainant, (iv) there are other means available to the complainant to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, or (v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator; or (b) if consideration of the complaint was suspended under subsection 241.1(1) and if, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice under subsection 241.1(2) were not taken within the specified period."

This comprehensive list covers situations where the Board finds the complaint invalid, lacking merit, or already resolved through other means.

### Circumstances Preventing Complaint

Section 251.01 outlines the conditions under which an employee may make a complaint. It states:
"(1) Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Head if they believe that the employer has contravened (a) any provision of this Part or of the regulations made under this Part; or (b) any order."

However, it also specifies limitations on making a complaint. Section 251.01(3.1) prohibits an employee from making a complaint based on substantially the same facts as a complaint previously made under certain subsections, unless that prior complaint has been withdrawn. This prevents repetitive complaints on the same issues.

Furthermore, Section 251.01(5) provides a greater certainty regarding complaints related to collective agreements:
"For greater certainty, a complaint is not permitted under this section if it relates to a disagreement whose settlement is governed exclusively by a collective agreement under subsection 168(1.1)."

This clarifies that complaints about issues already covered by a collective agreement are not allowed under this section.

### Assistance from the Head

Section 251.03 describes the Head's power to assist parties to a complaint to settle it:
"After receipt of a complaint, the Head may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint."

This indicates that the Head can intervene to facilitate a resolution between the parties, potentially preventing the need for suspension or rejection of the complaint.

### Extension of Time

Section 251.03(3) grants the Head the power to extend the time period specified in the notice for the complainant to take necessary measures:
"The Head may, upon request, extend the time period specified in the notice."

This provides flexibility for complainants who require additional time to fulfill the Board's requirements.

individual_results.question: What are the implications for an employee and an employer in terms of contributions to benefits during an employee's leave of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Implications for Employee and Employer Contributions to Benefits During Leave of Absence

### Accumulation of Benefits During Leave

Section 209.2(1) of the Canada Labour Code states,
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of any employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division shall accumulate during the entire period of the leave." This indicates a significant implication for both the employee and the employer. For the employee, it means that their benefits continue to accrue without interruption during the leave period. For the employer, it means that their contributions to these benefits continue as well, ensuring that the employee maintains their entitlements upon their return to work.

### Employee Responsibility for Contributions

Section 209.2(2) outlines the employee's responsibility for making contributions during a leave of absence. It says,
"Where contributions are required from an employee in order for the employee to be entitled to a benefit referred to in subsection (1), the employee is responsible for and must, within a reasonable time, pay those contributions for the period of any leave of absence under this Division unless, before taking leave or within a reasonable time thereafter, the employee notifies the employer of the employee’s intention to discontinue contributions during that period." This implies that even during a leave of absence, the employee remains responsible for making contributions if required to maintain their benefits. However, the employee has the right to notify the employer of their intention to discontinue contributions, provided they do so reasonably in advance.

### Employer Responsibility for Contributions

Section 209.2(2.1) clarifies the employer's obligation to continue making contributions during a leave of absence. It states,
"An employer who pays contributions in respect of a benefit referred to in subsection (1) shall continue to pay those contributions during an employee’s leave of absence under this Division in at least the same proportion as if the employee were not on leave unless the employee does not pay the employee’s contributions, if any, within a reasonable time." This means that the employer's contributions to benefits continue at the same rate as if the employee were still working, unless the employee informs the employer of their intention to discontinue contributions within a reasonable timeframe.

### Failure to Pay Contributions

Section 209.2(3) addresses the consequences of the employee failing to pay contributions during a leave of absence. It says,
"For the purposes of calculating the pension, health and disability benefits of an employee in respect of whom contributions have not been paid as required by subsections (2) and (2.1), the benefits shall not accumulate during the leave of absence and employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence." This indicates that if the employee does not pay their contributions, their benefits will not accumulate during the leave period, and their employment history will be considered continuous with their employment before the absence.

### Deemed Continuous Employment

Section 209.2(4) further clarifies the implications of failure to pay contributions on the calculation of benefits upon return to work. It states,
"For the purposes of calculating benefits of an employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division, other than benefits referred to in subsection (1), employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence." This means that even if the employee fails to pay their contributions during the leave, their employment history will be considered continuous with their employment before the absence for the purposes of calculating benefits upon their return.

individual_results.question: What information must an employer provide to redundant employees in writing, and by when, after giving notice of termination under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Information to Provide Redundant Employees

### Required Written Information

According to Section 213(2) of the Canada Labour Code, an employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must provide each redundant employee,
"...as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee, a statement in writing setting out, as at the date of the statement, his vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from his employment with that employer."

This quote directly addresses the question by specifying the exact information that must be provided in writing. It details the categories of information required: vacation benefits, wages, severance pay, and any other benefits and pay resulting from the employment. Furthermore, it sets a strict deadline for providing this information: no later than two weeks before the termination date.

### Timing of Provision

The Canada Labour Code clearly outlines the timeframe for providing this written statement. Section 213(2) states,
"...as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee..." This indicates a two-week window from the date the notice of group termination is given to the Head. The employer must provide the statement as soon as practically possible within this timeframe, but the absolute latest is two weeks prior to the termination date.

### Additional Information Required

Section 213(1) further elaborates on the information that must be provided to the Canada Employment Insurance Commission. It states,
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 and any trade union to which a copy of that notice is given must give the Canada Employment Insurance Commission any information requested by it for the purpose of assisting any redundant employee and must cooperate with the Commission to facilitate the re-establishment in employment of that employee." This implies that the employer must proactively share any information requested by the Canada Employment Insurance Commission to aid the redundant employees in finding new work.

### Cooperation with Commission

Section 213(1) also mandates cooperation with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission. It specifies that the employer must
"...cooperate with the Commission to facilitate the re-establishment in employment of that employee." This highlights the employer's responsibility to work with the Commission to support the redundant employees in their job search.

individual_results.question: Can a request for review of a notice of violation be escalated to a higher authority, and under what circumstances?

## Escalation of a Notice of Violation Review

### Circumstances for Escalation

Yes, a request for review of a notice of violation can be escalated to a higher authority, specifically the Board. This escalation occurs when the Head considers the request to be an appeal.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal, in which case the Head shall so inform the applicant and refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of this Part."

This passage explicitly states the condition under which a review request can be escalated. The Head has the discretion to treat the review request as an appeal. If the Head makes this determination, they must inform the applicant and forward the request to the Board. The Board then becomes the appellate body for the review.

### Process for Escalation

The process for escalating a review request to the Board involves the Head's decision to treat the request as an appeal.
"...the Head shall so inform the applicant and refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of this Part."

This indicates that the Head initiates the escalation by informing the applicant and submitting the request to the Board. The Board then assumes the role of the appellate authority, reviewing the Head's decision.

### Alternative Escalation: Request for Review as an Appeal

Another circumstance for escalation is when the Head considers the request for review to be an appeal, even without explicitly being prompted to do so.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal of their decision, in which case the Head shall so inform any person who is affected by the payment order, the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance — or, in the case of a compliance order, the employer — and shall refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of section 251.12."

This passage highlights the Head's discretionary power to escalate a review request as an appeal. If the Head deems it appropriate, they will inform the relevant parties and forward the request to the Board, which then acts as the appellate body.

### Request for Review as an Appeal in Other Contexts

The possibility of treating a review request as an appeal also arises in other contexts within the Canada Labour Code.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal of their decision, in which case the Head shall so inform any person who is affected by the payment order, the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance — or, in the case of a compliance order, the employer — and shall refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of section 251.12."

This reiterates the Head's discretion to escalate a review request as an appeal, even if not explicitly requested. The Board then becomes the appellate body.

### Request for Review as an Appeal in Payment Order Reviews

The option to treat a review request as an appeal also applies to reviews of payment orders.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal of their decision, in which case the Head shall so inform any person who is affected by the payment order, the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance — or, in the case of a compliance order, the employer — and shall refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of section 251.12."

This passage confirms that the Head can escalate a review request as an appeal when considering a payment order. The Board then acts as the appellate authority.

individual_results.question: In cases where an employee complains about an employer's action related to certain rights, who bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that the alleged contravention did or did not occur?
individual_results.answer:
## Burden of Proof in Complaints Against Employers

### Section 133(6) of the Canada Labour Code
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party."

This section directly addresses the question by establishing the burden of proof in complaints made to the Board. It states that the very fact of filing a complaint under section 133 serves as evidence that the alleged contravention *did* occur. Therefore, if a party to the complaint proceedings disputes this, the onus is on *that* party to prove that the contravention did *not* happen. This signifies a shift in the burden of proof when a complaint is lodged, placing it squarely on the employer to demonstrate the absence of the alleged violation.

### Section 133(6) and the Exercise of Rights

The quoted passage further clarifies the application of this burden of proof specifically when an employee exercises a right under sections 128 or 129. It emphasizes that the complaint itself is evidence of the contravention. Consequently, if an employer challenges the occurrence of the contravention, the employer bears the burden of proving that it did not happen. This underscores the protective nature of the complaint process, where the mere filing of a complaint provides a presumption of the employer's wrongdoing, requiring the employer to rebut that presumption.

### Section 6.2 of the Canada Labour Code
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

While this section doesn't specifically address complaints to the Board, it establishes a general rule regarding the burden of proof when an employer disputes an employee's status. It states that if an employer claims a person is not their employee in any proceeding other than a prosecution, the employer bears the burden of proving that the person is not their employee. This principle is consistent with the burden of proof established in section 133(6) for complaints to the Board, where the employer must prove the contravention did not occur if the employee files a complaint.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can the maximum hours of work for an employee in a week be adjusted or have exceptions?

## Conditions for Adjusting or Having Exceptions to Maximum Hours of Work

### Emergency Work
"In case of emergency, such as an accident or essential work on equipment, an employer may exceed the maximum hours of work without a permit." This section outlines a primary condition under which the standard maximum hours can be adjusted. It states that employers can exceed the maximum hours in emergency situations, but this requires a report to the Head and, if applicable, the trade union within 15 days of the end of the month in which the employee(s) worked emergency hours. The report must detail the nature of the emergency, the number of employees working in excess of the maximum hours, and the number of additional hours each employee worked.

### Averaging
"In some establishments, the nature of work necessitates irregular hours of work due to seasonal or other factors. This means that as an employee, you may be subject to:   scheduled hours that vary from time to time, or no regularly scheduled hours  If this applies to you, your employer may average your hours of work over a period of 2 or more weeks. As such, standard and maximum hours would be calculated across a period of 2 or more weeks rather than on a daily or weekly basis." This section describes another condition for adjusting maximum hours: averaging. It explains that in certain workplaces with irregular hours, employers can average an employee's hours over a period of two or more weeks. This means that the standard and maximum hours are calculated on a bi-weekly basis rather than a daily or weekly basis.

### Excess Hour Permit
"...the maximum hours of work can be exceeded:  under an excess hour permit..." This point directly addresses an exception to the standard maximum hours. It states that employers can exceed the maximum hours under an excess hour permit, which is obtained in emergency situations.

### Averaging Plan

"For emergency work under an averaging plan." This further clarifies the application of averaging as an exception. It specifies that averaging plans can be used for emergency work.

### Modified Work Schedule
"...can be exceeded:  under an excess hour permit  for emergency work under an averaging plan under a modified work schedule..." This section expands on the application of averaging as an exception, specifically mentioning its use in modified work schedules. It states that the maximum hours can be exceeded under an averaging plan within a modified work schedule.

### Exemptions from and Modifications to Hours of Work Provisions Regulations
"As an employee, and subject to the Exemptions from and Modifications to Hours of Work Provisions Regulations, you are entitled to a break, rest period, notice of work schedule and notice of a shift change, as detailed below." This refers to a set of regulations that provide further exemptions and modifications to the standard maximum hours. It indicates that employees are entitled to certain breaks and notices under these regulations.

### Specific Employee Classes
"Regulations set out exemptions from or modifications to what maximum hours of work is for certain classes of employees:  drivers in the trucking industry (Motor Vehicle Operators Hours of Work Regulations) employees on ships in the East Coast and Great Lakes shipping industry (East Coast and Great Lakes Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations, 1985) and the West Coast shipping industry (West Coast Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations) running trades employees in the railway industry (Railway Running-Trades Employees Hours of Work Regulations) the commission salespersons in the broadcasting industry (Broadcasting Industry Commission Salesmen Hours of Work Regulations), and the commission-paid salespeople in the banking industry (Banking Industry Commission-paid Salespeople Hours of Work Regulations)..." This section details specific employee classes that have exemptions or modifications to the standard maximum hours. It lists several examples, including truck drivers, ship employees in various regions, railway running trades employees, broadcasting commission salespersons, and banking commission-paid salespeople.
